purpose: Game-ready core family vocabulary for every canonical learn-from language. Each semantic slot may have one or several valid realizations; multiple forms preserve distinctions such as age, parental side, speaker gender, or regional/common alternatives instead of forcing a fake one-word equivalence.

concept_contract.family: the family/household-kin group as a general beginner topic label
concept_contract.brother: male sibling; languages may split by relative age or speaker gender
concept_contract.sister: female sibling; languages may split by relative age or speaker gender
concept_contract.grandfather: male grandparent; languages may split maternal/paternal side
concept_contract.grandmother: female grandparent; languages may split maternal/paternal side
concept_contract.uncle: a parent's brother / conventional uncle relation; languages may split side and relative age
concept_contract.aunt: a parent's sister / conventional aunt relation; languages may split side and relative age
concept_contract.cousin: cousin relation; languages may split gender, parental side, or lineage

realization_policy: A forms array is not a synonym list unless the forms really overlap. It may encode a language's required semantic split.
Games must use relationship clues compatible with the selected form. Do not ask a broad English-style question when the target language requires age, side, speaker gender, or another distinction.
A conventional or descriptive phrase is valid when the language has no single lexical item for the broad concept.
Generated forms are machine-draft candidates. Structural game readiness does not equal linguistic review or certification.
Do not import or copy Wiktionary/KinDiv word rows. External kinship typology research informs the semantic model only.
source_refs: Khishigsuren et al. 2022, Using Linguistic Typology to Enrich Multilingual Lexicons: the Case of Lexical Gaps in Kinship
